title: L.A. County Hits 100 West Nile Cases, Highest in Nearly a Decade
excerpt: One hundred infections, 94 hospitalizations and five deaths put Los Angeles County on its worst West Nile pace since 2017, with weeks of mosquito season still ahead.
body:
• Los Angeles County has reported 100 West Nile virus infections in 2026, its highest count this early in the season since 2017 — already more than four times all of 2025's total of 22.
  • Of the 100 patients, 94 were hospitalized and five have died. One-third live in the East Los Angeles area.
  • The milestone tracks a statewide surge: California reports its highest West Nile activity in five years, with the U.S. total at 671 cases across 42 states.
  • Mosquito season runs through November, so weeks of exposure remain. Officials urge insect repellent, eliminating standing water and keeping window screens fitted.

Los Angeles County is facing its worst West Nile virus season in nearly a decade. The county Department of Public Health announced Monday that 100 infections have been reported in 2026 — the highest number recorded this early in the mosquito season since 2017, when 268 cases were tallied over the full year. The current total already exceeds the county's full-year counts for every year from 2018 through 2025, and is more than four times the 22 infections reported in all of 2025.

The severity is as striking as the count. Of the 100 infections listed by the county, 94 involved hospitalization and five people have died. Ninety-six of the 100 cases were symptomatic, with the most recent onset of illness on Sept. 4. Geographically, about a third of infected patients live in the East Los Angeles area, roughly a quarter in the San Fernando Valley and about a fifth in the South Bay. The county's figures exclude cases reported separately by Long Beach and Pasadena.

How the season escalated

The climb has been fast. The county announced its first human case in July — an Antelope Valley resident hospitalized with West Nile encephalitis. By Aug. 20, state health officials were already warning that West Nile activity across California had reached a five-year high. A little more than a month later, Los Angeles County alone hit 100 confirmed infections.

The environmental surveillance underneath the human numbers is even more striking. California has confirmed 3,001 West Nile-positive mosquito samples from 29 counties and 481 positive dead birds from 23 counties this year. Public health officials note that the virus circulates between birds and mosquitoes for weeks before it reaches people — a county with heavy mosquito positivity and few human cases is better read as early than spared.

"Public health officials have been warning that rising temperatures have allowed mosquitoes to thrive, increasing the risk of the diseases they spread, including West Nile."

— County and state health officials, in the September case announcement

What the disease does

West Nile is the leading cause of mosquito-borne disease in the continental United States, according to the CDC. Mosquitoes become infected after feeding on infected birds, then spread the virus to humans and other animals. About one in five infected people develops symptoms — fever, headache, body aches, vomiting, diarrhea or rash — while most never know they were infected. About one in 150 develops severe disease: encephalitis or meningitis, which can lead to paralysis or death. Older adults and people with conditions such as cancer, high blood pressure or kidney disease face the greatest risk, though people of any age can become infected.

There are no licensed vaccines or medications for West Nile. Each year roughly 2,000 Americans are diagnosed, a figure the CDC believes is an undercount because most infections are mild or asymptomatic. Nationally, 671 cases have been reported across 42 states this year, and the true number is likely higher because cases peak in August and September and reporting lags.

Weeks of exposure remain

Los Angeles County's mosquito season generally runs from June through November, which means residents face weeks of potential exposure even as the weather cools. Officials are urging the standard toolkit: use insect repellent, wear long sleeves and pants during outdoor activity, keep windows and doors fitted with screens, use air conditioning, and empty containers with standing water where mosquitoes breed.

For the Indian diaspora across the county — concentrated heavily in the very East L.A. and San Fernando Valley areas carrying the largest case shares — the arithmetic of this season is simple: one in five infections produces symptoms, but among those that do, this year's cases are hospitalizing nearly everyone. Anyone who feels ill after mosquito exposure, especially with fever, headache, body aches or rash, should contact a health professional; severe headache, stiff neck, confusion or muscle weakness warrant urgent care.
